en: Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán of the Tang Dynasty.
Regarding the section on those of "Fewer Knowledge," not only is no praise offered nor their names listed, but this is because few people know them.
As for the mention of "sages and ordinary beings" and so forth, it explains the reason why they are categorized as having fewer knowledge.
Because ordinary people cannot fathom the Sage, it is said that "intercourse is severed.

It is not that the Sage does not interact with ordinary people at all that this is called severance; rather, it is understood when one considers the interaction between ordinary people as ordinary people. How much more so when considering the principle that intercourse must be severed when an ordinary person looks toward the Sage? Once such friendly intercourse is severed, how could it be a matter of the degree of one's understanding?

Regarding the phrase "Specifically because," etc.: Now, the Sage, in order to lead ordinary beings and inspire those of a similar type, accommodates them according to their differing capacities and conditions. Thus, he manifests traces of limited consciousness to receive those who possess hidden virtues; for this reason, he does not judge the high or low status of what is known or cognized based on whether an ordinary person can know or cognize it.
Therefore, one must not lose sight of the fundamental by focusing on the traces of quantity; likewise, one must not consider the extent of one's knowledge to be the measure of high or low status.

Furthermore, one cannot claim that having many acquaintances constitutes a real basis while having few acquaintances constitutes no real basis; therefore, we know that both many acquaintances and few acquaintances are merely superficial traces (*traces*), whereas there exists a distinct underlying rational basis. If this underlying basis is enduring, it possesses its own inherent reality and fulfillment.
If one wishes to distinguish the four *siddhāntas* within this context: "Because there are differences in quantity" refers to the worldly (*loka-*) level;
"in accordance with the capacities of beings" refers to the personal (*pudgala-*) level;
"concealing the name to hide its virtue" refers to the remedial (*pratipakṣa-*) level; and "its height and depth cannot be measured" refers to the ultimate (*paramārtha-*) level.
Regarding the phrase "the eighteen types of practitioners of the Tripiṭaka," this is fully explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.
As for the two sections that distinguish between the stages of training and no-more-training, the former pertains to the Two Vehicles, while the latter pertains to Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the former section was based on the common stages of the three vehicles, while the latter was based on the exclusive stage of the bodhisattva.

Within the Distinct and Perfect teachings as well, there are two divisions: the first, "with effort and without effort," refers to the stages prior to and following the [first] ground; the second, "possessing and not possessing," refers to Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment. Although the initial entry into the state of effortless practice may also be termed "beyond-learning" (aśaikṣa), this is because it is only partially attained; therefore, the term is further applied here in its full sense.
The intention behind citing the *Āgama* is to open the thematic lead for the third proposition.
As for why the opponent poses this question: "If you say that an Arhat is already 'beyond training' (*aśaikṣa*), for what reason must they still follow after the World-Honored One?"
The passage beginning with "If that were so" poses a hypothetical question to raise the point; the answer therein constitutes the fourth category.

Generally speaking, those called "learners" (*śaikṣa*) are so designated for the purpose of further progress toward abandonment. Thus, those such as the *saptakṛtparama*, the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) no longer have anything left to learn. If one progresses through the fruits [of the path], this logically belongs to the preceding categories; how much more so for one who has already abandoned what was to be abandoned and has nothing further to abandon, who certainly belongs to the fourth category.
Furthermore, the "neither-nor" [category] consists of five propositions. This applies to the Śrāvakas of both teachings alike.
Regarding the analogy for the four teachings, specifically concerning the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*):

the first two propositions are as previously stated. As for the latter two propositions, because those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) abide in their respective stages, the one beyond training cannot further train; thus, the one beyond training remains as such. However, when the one beyond training manifests in the world of appearances (*nirmāṇa*), they are termed "in training," while they should actually regress to take the sixth stage as their state of being beyond training.
If one follows the analogy of the Arhat, the Buddha likewise abides in wholesome dharmas as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who is still training;

yet, in the final stages of the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles], one must simply not allow the Buddha to have anything further to learn, which would result in the omission of the third phrase—this can be understood by analogy with the Shared [Vehicle].
Furthermore, by taking the stage of ordinary beings as the fifth phrase, the latter three teachings each possess two sections, all resulting in five phrases.

Regarding the statement in the *Benji* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) that "one dwells in the śaikṣa and aśaikṣa stages of the *pūrṇākṣara* [complete letter] teaching," both the Separate and Complete Teachings take the stage of those who have not yet reached fulfillment; within this, it does not preclude the presence of ancient Buddhas, who are precisely the aśaikṣas of the second section.

Furthermore, regarding the character "full" (man): "full" pervades the three teachings, yet by distinguishing between two and following the one that is perfect (yuan), it refers specifically to the Perfect Teaching.

When it says, "Sentient beings should adorn the twin trees with the 'half-words' of those in training and those beyond training," this means first being led from the half-words into the perfection [of the teaching]. This is like the withered trees shown at the Deer Park and the flourishing trees shown in the Vaipulya (fangdeng) period; at that time, they were already adorned as non-dual. Those who initially practiced while clinging to the traces were ignorant of the fundamental source; it was only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras that the truth was finally revealed. Thus, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, six individuals are cited as causes who, having realized their Buddha-nature, are identical to the Tathāgata; because these two are non-dual, they are called "adorned."

Having already established two phrases—“learner” (śaikṣa) and “non-learner” (aśaikṣa)—within the contemplation of the mind, one should further establish two more phrases: that which contemplates without an object is called "non-learner," and constantly contemplating in this manner is called "learner. This forms the fifth phrase in relation to those who have not yet practiced; alternatively, it may be established as the fifth phrase according to principle. Thus, each of the three contemplations can individually constitute five phrases, which can be seen by reflecting upon this.

Regarding the statement in the *Zhongguan* (Treatise on the Middle) that "if one discusses the realms (*dhātu*) and suchnesses (*tathatā*) in mutual relation, they total two thousand," the "hundred realms and thousand suchnesses" would merely constitute one thousand; this is because there are ten realms within the hundred realms, and each realm possesses ten suchnesses. Furthermore, one should also apply the hundred suchnesses across the thousand realms.
It is also called "one thousand. For instance, if the ten suchnesses (shí rú) were to exist as ten sets of ten, they would constitute one hundred suchnesses;

when these are applied to the ten realms, would this not be one thousand realms? This is merely a provisional discussion of their single numbers. However, within the one thousand realms of the hundred suchnesses, each realm contains ten realms, and within the one thousand suchnesses of the hundred realms, each suchness contains ten suchnesses; how could it be that there are merely one thousand realms and one thousand suchnesses respectively?
These are thus layered and inexhaustible, such that they cannot be numbered or known; how then could one fix them at a definite number of two thousand?
Therefore, it is said they are "inconceivable.
Since this applies to all objects of experience, and is stated here merely for convenience, it is referred to as "two thousand."

In the section on the provisional teachings based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*), the enumerations are simply listed; for the purpose of the meaning, this is sufficient and there is no need to seek anything further. Therefore, the preceding two passages merely list them directly.

If one wishes to establish the meaning such that hearing these enumerations brings joy, generates wholesome roots, destroys evil, and leads into the Truth—this is precisely the intent behind the different interpretations of the applications of contemplation (*guan*) and their corresponding enumerations across the various teachings.

Regarding the phrase "Manifesting the Trace" (*jǔ jì*) and below, this refers to the relationship between the Original (*běn*) and the Trace (*jì*). As for "Manifesting the Trace" and so forth: these very phenomena of the Trace are themselves the Dharma of the Original.

Because the Original inherently possesses a trace, it is called "Original-Trace"; yet, without the trace, there would be no means to manifest the Original. This trace is precisely the trace of the Original House; because without the Original there would be no means to suspend the trace, therefore, among the two thousand traces, each is a trace within the two thousand originals, and this applies throughout the higher and lower realms alike.
The resolution of this objection is as previously explained regarding the section on "those with many acquaintances.

Concerning the statement in the listing of the community of nuns, "Furthermore, there is no textual evidence," etc., which refutes the old interpretation: at the conclusion of the section on the community of bhikṣus, it is stated, "Because they are thus well-known to the assembly, they may be called 'many'"; however, at the conclusion of the sections on those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no such concluding remark. Therefore, compared to the former case where they were "many," they are here referred to as "few."

Regarding the two texts concerning the *bhikṣuṇī* community: since there is no mention of them being "well-known to the assembly" at the beginning, nor any basis for considering them "few" at the end, they are said to be "without textual record.

As for the phrase "the meaning is untenable," this refers to how one determines whether [a person] is widely known or little known based on the *bhikṣu* community’s praise or lack of praise of their virtues, the inclusion or exclusion of their names, the number of individuals listed, and the presence or absence of a formal conclusion.

Now, within the assembly of nuns, only the names of the two leaders are specified; after those two, it merely says "six thousand" and "together with their retinues," without any further enumeration. How could it be that while six thousand are recognized by others, the retinues themselves are not recognized?
Since he does not even rank among those whose names are hidden in the treasury of virtue, how can it be said that his [attainments] are few?
As for the terms "great" and "small," these refer to the old designations of "great fame" and "small fame," which have already been refuted as previously stated.
Furthermore, "Yaśodharā" is translated as "Renowned" (Yiming); how could it be claimed, on the contrary, that she lacked renown?

Regarding the two nuns, the lack of an explanation according to the teachings (yuejiao) should be supplemented by analogy; likewise, they should also be explained according to the monastic requisites (sengju) in terms of the four teachings and five flavors.
Question:
Why is the name Mahāprajāpatī explained by means of the *Prajñāpāramitā* to eliminate its original meaning?
Furthermore, since she is not the Mother of the Buddha, why is she cited and explained by reference to the Mother of the Buddha?
Answer:

It is because one possesses wisdom that one is able to love the Way; since one loves the Great Way, the Wisdom-Perfection (Prajñāpāramitā) is likewise great. Furthermore, while ordinary women are all capable of giving birth to children, [the practitioner] here borrows the Mother from the Dharma-gate of Vimalakīrti to give birth to the Son of the Guide within their own mind. The numerical counts and the general meaning of the provisional teachings are as explained previously.

Regarding the enumeration within the "Contemplation" chapter where the six sense organs are treated as six thousand, although this borrows from the text of the subsequent "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," here it is intended to apply universally across both the beginning and the end [of the Lotus Sutra]. If these were strictly restricted to the female assembly, they would all belong to the stage of sages whose six sense organs have already received their predictions (vyākaraṇa) during the three weeks; therefore, when using the ten kinds of six sense organs from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to represent the fundamental dharma-gate, it simultaneously encompasses the meaning of both the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku).

Regarding Yaśodharā’s designation as “the mother by means of her son”: generally, whether one designates parents by their children or children by their parents, it is permissible to use them to manifest one another provided that they possess virtuous deeds recognized by others; this applies to all bhikṣus as well.

Regarding the statement, "Some say there is no equivalent translation," this does not apply to Yaśodharā alone; rather, among all untranslated terms, many possess both equivalents and non-equivalents, as exemplified by the term *sūtra* and others.
Regarding "the Buddha’s wife," this is a case of explaining the cause by means of the fruit.
Since he had already renounced Yaśodharā at the time of his departure from home, there was no longer any wife when the title of "Buddha" was attained.

Regarding the three ladies as symbols of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*): Mṛgajā symbolizes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) because she was not born; Yaśodharā symbolizes the provisional (*upādāya-prajñapti*) because she was born; and since she dwells between these two contemplations, Mahāprajāpatī’s position is clearly shown to represent the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Below the section “The Superior Portion,” the text clarifies the contemplation of mind regarding both the original and the trace; herein, it first explains the purpose of its inclusion, followed by the formal exposition.
The former consists of two parts:
first, the general, and second, the specific.

Regarding the general clarification in the first two phrases: the two characters "dang-fen" (當分) are both pronounced in the departing tone. The reason they are used together to clarify the contemplation of the mind in terms of the fundamental and the trace is that while causes and conditions cannot be explained as being combined, they should be mutually interpenetrated according to the principles of the teachings; now, wishing to discuss them together as primary and attendant, it is for the sake of convenience in contemplating the mind through the fundamental and the trace.

However, regarding the various assemblies of bodhisattvas, each has its own fundamental and manifest aspects; as for the observation that their minds are not shared with those who are enlightened, this is because their outward forms and attire are coarse, they have no beginning or end, they do not regard material things as important, and it is not because the sutras treat them as distinct.

Furthermore, as for the reason why the characteristics of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) are not explained separately: from the fundamental [manifestation] down to the provisional traces (*traces*), there is nothing but response and resonance (*ganying*). Since that which is enacted through response and resonance does not exceed the characteristics of the teachings, the two other aspects [the principle and the practice] are naturally subsumed within the fundamental and the trace.
If this is so, since these two points have already been addressed above, why is it necessary to clarify them again?
Answer:

Because the conditions for transformation differ, there is nothing that does not benefit sentient beings. Since causes and conditions are interrelated, traces must be established in concert—whether one person relates to many, many relate to one, one relates to one, or many relate to many. Thus, from beginning to end, through the interplay of intimacy and distance, primary and secondary figures, and the manifest and the secret, they together constitute a single transformation.

Furthermore, in the contemplative practice of the noble ones, within a single kṣaṇa, the observer and the observed encompass an entire lifetime—including phenomena and principle, the provisional and the real, persons and dharmas, the principal and its attendants, the hidden and the manifest, and the good and the evil—all of which are subsumed by this mental contemplation. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify this by way of the "king" (the primary subject).
Next, from "Manifesting Skillful Means" (*kṣānti-upāya*) onwards, the specific intent of the coming [of the teaching] is described.
The first phrase clarifies the intent of the coming of the fundamental and the trace; the second phrase clarifies the intent of the coming of the contemplation of the mind.

It is called "skillful" (*kuśala*) because it is the most excellent among skillful means. It is called "curved and clever" (*vakra-vidagdha*) because there is not a single sage who does not accord with the capacities and conditions of beings. It is called "refined and subtle" (*sūkṣma-praṇīta*) because there is not a single moment of mind that does not constitute wondrous contemplation. It is "curved" because it accords with capacities; it is "clever" because it guides and encourages; it is "refined" because it is unmixed; and it is "subtle" because the principle reaches its ultimate limit.

From the phrase "Now, regarding the *Śūraṅgama*," there is first a general explanation of the primary and secondary manifestations (*honji-suijaku*) in three parts: first, an account of the descent of the traces to discuss in general the way of benefiting sentient beings; second, from "Now, for the time being" onwards, clarifying how the principal and attendants share the same intention regarding the methods of transformation; third, from "By this" onwards, summarizing the merit of the samādhi.
First, it clarifies the basis for both the fundamental and the manifested; the fundamental ground is the *Śūraṅgama*, while the manifestation is its provisional display.
"Appropriateness" clarifies the intent behind manifesting these traces.
The phrase "there is nothing [that remains]" clarifies the manifestation of the traces [of the Buddha's descent].

In various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, it is explained that the Arhats attain only the four types of knowledge; they are merely subject to rebuke and purification, yet the underlying intent of such transformation is not clarified. At that time, who would say that their aggregates of birth are not yet exhausted, their holy life not yet established, or their task not yet accomplished, while there still remains the state of change and transformation? Therefore, we know that "exhaustion" is explained here solely in reference to the realm within the triple world.

Once [the truth] has been revealed, it is seen that [the Buddha] was originally a great master of expedient means (*mahopāya-kauśalya*); therefore, he first followed the ways of the non-Buddhists and then the Hinayana to lead beings into the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). Thus, it would not have been possible to manifest his traces of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*) without this fundamental *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. This is why it is said: "There is nothing he does not do."
Next, the clarification of the principal figures, their retinues, and the regions of transformation consists of six parts:
first, the descent of the spirits of the principal figures and their retinues;
second, from "If thirty-two... onwards, the clarification of the birth of the teacher and his disciples.
Three: "If [they are] illustrious" and below clarifies that they collectively receive the worldly path; Four:
"If [it is] the Dharma" and below clarifies the ripening of the producer and the produced, specifically referring to the Small Vehicle of the Deer Park; Five:

"Collectively assisting" and below further ripens those who are not yet ripened, specifically referring to the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā; Six: "Next, hearing the Lotus Sūtra" and below clarifies that the merit of the principal and its attendants is complete.
The first section also has two parts:
the first is the principal [subject], and the second, beginning with "Dharmakāya," is the retinue.
The subsequent passage also has two parts:
The first section concerns the teachers; next, from "the various great [beings]" downward, it concerns the disciples.
The third passage also has two parts:
first, the teachers demonstrate their adherence to worldly paths; second, from "the various great beings" downward, it demonstrates their subsequent reception of heterodox teachings.
The fourth passage also has two parts:
first, knowing that those to be converted are still in the stage of birth; second, from "If those... onwards, discerning that the faculties of those to be converted have matured.
The fifth passage also has two parts:
First is the Vaipulya, followed by the Prajñā.
The sixth section also has two parts:
first, the formal clarification that the task is completed; second, from the words "Dharma King" onwards, a reiteration of the Half and Full [Teachings] to manifest the merit of the transformation.
The division of the text is complete; next, I shall provide a brief commentary.
Regarding the term "proximate treatise" (*upadeśa*), we shall temporarily set aside the intermediate stages to discuss Gayā.
As for the "Noble Queen," she was the consort of the Holy Sovereign; she is also called "Queen" because her governance was virtuous.

Regarding the phrase "Dharmakāya" and so forth: there are also ancient Buddhas who are referred to as Bodhisattvas; when the principal [Buddha] has descended into the world, his companions likewise appear in the traces [of manifestation].
"Golden form" refers to a beautiful countenance of golden hue.
Regarding the term "Mahāsattva" (Great Being): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to a bodhisattva as a mahāsattva, also called an ādikarmika (Opening Being).
"Sattva" (Being) is a general designation for a person; by qualifying it with "great" (*mahā*) or "opening" (*ādi*), they are thus termed "Great Beings" and so forth.

Just as in the world one uses terms such as "benevolent person" (renshi) or "aspirant" (zhishi) to distinguish individuals by their benevolence and other qualities, so too here one distinguishes them by their benevolence and so forth.

Now, those among humanity who give rise to the Great Mind are called "Great"; "opening" (kai) is another name for "giving rise to" (fa). Because they lead different types of beings, their various characteristics differ accordingly.
"An empty room," Subhūti, refers to the fact that at the time of birth, everything within the room was empty, signifying the realization of emptiness.
"Raining jewels" refers to Rāhula.
Regarding the phrase "Entrusting the Discernment of Dreams": this refers to Śāriputra. As for the term "Crown Prince" and so forth:

initially they were the same, but later they became different; because [the Buddha] wished to take back what he had first given, he acted as an emperor and the like. Occupying the position of supreme honor, he served as the precursor. As the *Caiguojing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states:

"When the Buddha was about to descend to this Jambudvīpa, there were ninety-nine billion followers. He abandoned these great multitudes and forgot the four continents; therefore, it says "abandoned the kingdom. Because he relinquished the rank of the Golden Wheel-turning King, it says "renounced kingship. Because he demonstrated the practice of worldly meditative concentrations, it says "studied the Way. Because various great beings likewise demonstrated receiving false teachings, it says "requested instruction. Because he surpassed what others had practiced, it says "comprehensively proficient. Because he subsequently gathered those followers, it says "patriarchal master."

Just as Śāriputra’s sixteen-fold voice resounded throughout the five regions, he and Maudgalyāyana studied under the same teacher, the brahmin Śāraṇa; before even ten days had passed, Śāraṇa entrusted his entire assembly of disciples to them.
When the Great Dharma was about to be inaugurated, he first acted as its pioneer, like Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others;
once those to be converted had been brought forth, the converter still maintained an equal footing with them, like Mahākāśyapa and others.
"Resistance" (*kàng*) is as the *Yi* says:
"To know how to advance but not how to retreat; to know how to gain but not how to lose.
It is also "confrontation" (*duì*); because he was unwilling to serve as a minister, he divided the courtyard and would not withdraw.
Regarding the phrase "venerating the truth of my Way," it is just as in the case of Kāśyapa.
Because their faculties were matured within the conditions [of their encounter] and were ready for transformation, it is said that they were "easily influenced" and so forth.
Each of the great beings held a specific office: Śāriputra possessed wisdom; Maudgalyāyana possessed supernormal powers; Kātyāyana possessed eloquence; and Pūrṇa possessed samādhi.

Regarding the phrase "further delivering those not yet delivered": although the teacher and disciples have received transformation and the path of transformation has not ceased, "delivering" carries two meanings. If they have not yet fully received transformation, then within the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings, one further causes them to enter the Hīnayāna; if they are bodhisattvas, one merely causes them to exhaust their ignorance.

Regarding the phrase "having already matured through repeated maturation," since the two stages of maturation—great and small—have not yet reached their conclusion, it is logically necessary to enter [the next stage].

In the *Shimu Dazhong* (Explanation of the Great Yearning), the term "not knowing" refers precisely to this state where the great capacity (*mahāyāna-śakti*) is secretly activated; this is the same meaning as what follows below regarding the "two searches of capacity and emotion."

Regarding the term "containing and embracing" (*hanjie*) and so forth: it refers to the fact that within the Prajñā [Pāramitā] teachings, the two vehicles of the Shared Teaching are included. Thus, because within those sections of the Shared Teaching, the true Middle Way possesses both the Great and the Small Vehicles, it is called "containing" (*han*);
because the Great Vehicle encompasses the Small, it is called "embracing" (*jie*); and because it extends through both the Great and the Small from beginning to end, it is so designated.
Regarding the phrase "giving and taking" (*chūnai*) and so forth, this clarifies the reception of karma, because it causes both oneself and others to understand all dharmas.
The details of giving and taking are explained as set forth in the sub-commentary (*sho*).
Regarding the two characters "chū" (out) and "nai" (in), those in the region south of the Yangtze River mostly pronounce them with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), and this is not without reason.
If one considers the act of a person entering or exiting, the character for "chū" may follow the entering tone (*rùshēng*), while the movement performed by the person may follow the departing tone.
As for the character "nai," its meaning is identical in both the northern and southern pronunciations; however, fearing confusion with the word "wài" (outside), it follows the southern pronunciation.
"Common" refers to the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-śāsana).
If this is so, why is it not entrusted to the Piṭaka?
Answer:
This has already been obtained previously.
"Distinct" refers to the Distinct and the Perfect; the details regarding the partial and the perfect are as distinguished in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).
Being "entrusted with a command" is termed "receiving and understanding"; the act of speaking is called "receiving," for there is no separate act of receiving apart from the speech itself.

Abiding still in the minor fruits is called "having no longing for acquisition"; transforming into the refined butter is called "not yet suddenly relinquishing"; looking toward the ultimate teaching that follows is called "although"; and having one's mind remain unstartled when receiving the bestowed teachings is called "serene and expansive."
Therefore, the term "gradually" applies to the past, while "thoroughly refined" refers exclusively to matured butter.
"Next, hearing the Lotus Sūtra" clarifies reaching the fifth period, as explained in detail within the "Expedient Means" (Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta) chapter.
Because the true body is manifested, one accords with the nature of heaven; because the nature of heaven is fixed, the principle of father and son is established.
In the past, when the great vow was formed, it was called the "true body"; upon receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), the principle of father and son was established.
It was only after [the Buddha] had served twenty thousand Buddhas in the past that he became fit for the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Because solitary practice leads to *nirvāṇa*, it is called "extinguishing alone" (*ekamuni*); since there is not even a single person who extinguishes alone, how could many people be left behind?
Below "Dharma King," the intent behind the teachings of a single lifetime is further described.

Below "Initially Employing," the concepts of the Half and Full [Teachings] and withering and flourishing are borrowed to accomplish the work of transformation, thereby explaining the aforementioned terms "expedient means" and "skillful artifice."

Because his great transformative work was completed, he is called "Śāriputra" and so forth; because he did not wait for *nirvāṇa*, it is said that he "ceased his transformation. "Ransoming one's life" is as explained in the *Shiqian*.

If one were to interpret it according to this explanation, even when interpreting the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra* through both the general and specific aspects of its primary and trace manifestations (*honji-suijaku*), one would still fear failing to grasp the essential intent; how much less so when it is merely a single phrase that translates a name—how does this differ from the assemblies of śrāvakas in the other teachings?

Regarding the phrase "proclaiming extinction" (*nirvāṇa-ghoṣa*) and so forth: it is precisely because the proclamation of extinction arises upon the completion of one's task that the conditions for proclaiming extinction lie within this very scripture.

Regarding the phrase "twenty thousand lamps of light" and so forth: according to Mañjuśrī’s response to the question, he cites what he previously saw; since there was no subsequent teaching [beyond that], one should know that his transformation was completed at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for what was seen in the eastern direction—where both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* were fully witnessed—it is because those instances are cited as being identical to the present Buddha.

If Kāśyapa appears in the world, his land will likewise be pure; the principle is the same as when he went to see [the Buddha]. Although there is a difference regarding whether he has entered *nirvāṇa* or not, both cases manifest the reality (*tattva*) within this sutra.
Regarding the phrase "those who study" and so forth: men such as Ratnakūṭa and Śubhavyūha, and women such as Candrottarā and Vimaladattā.

"Path" refers to the two groups of the ordained; "lay" refers to the two groups of the laity. These four factors—initiation and so forth—are present in all of them, extending even to the noble and the lowly, humans and animals, the near and the distant, the respectful and the arrogant, the angry and the joyful, and the ordinary and the sage; since their characteristics are not uniform, it is annotated as "and so forth."

Next, regarding the "General Explanation of the Contemplations": the general and specific outlines have been explained in detail as previously stated. Twenty mental factors (*caitasika*) collectively assist the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) in perceiving wholesome objects; just as when first initiating contemplation, one does not depart from the categories of the mind-king, so too these mental factors universally lead one through to the realm of the wholesome. By means of these great wholesome factors encountering various conditions and objects, their wholesomeness becomes increasingly profound, as seen in the present sutra. Therefore, these wholesome factors have no separate ontological substance; they arise simply by transforming the unwholesome factors. Thus, one enters the small from the external, and the large from the small; only when returning from the beginning to the end is it called the ultimate excellence of the wholesome. Although wholesome practices are numerous, they do not exceed these ten; hence it is said, "The ten minds are the foundation."

Once the transformation has reached its limit, it returns to being identical with the mind-king (cittarāja), which is neither good nor evil; just as when the various disciples have received their predictions of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), they become partially identical with the Dharma King, and thus it is said that they are "established."

Furthermore, "gradual transformation" refers to those such as the śrāvakas, while "sudden transformation" refers to those such as the sudden-awakening bodhisattvas; none of these fail to accord with the true mark (dharmatā). This causes the King to achieve the ultimate Dharma and the Prince to become a true son of the Dharma-King, both becoming capable of succeeding to the position and transforming future lives. Therefore, among these, one first takes up the wholesome mind; however, what is listed here now follows the old translations.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (New Translation) states: "Faith (*śraddhā*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), the two faculties (*indriya*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)—diligence (*vīrya*) alone is universal to all wholesome minds.

The first three phrases list the individual terms one by one, while the final four characters provide the summary. If one wishes to briefly distinguish the similarities and differences between these new names and their traditional counterparts: the "faith" mentioned in the new translation refers to the acceptance and conviction regarding the Triple Gem; thus, its meaning is identical to the traditional name.

The new translation calls it "heedfulness" (*apramāda*); this refers to the nature of cultivating all virtues with focused attention. The old translation calls it "mindfulness" (*smṛti*); "mindfulness" means to remember and maintain, so while the names differ, the meaning is the same.

The new term "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) refers to a nature that is light, agile, comfortable, and capable; the old term was "joy" (*prīti*). Joy is a state of delight and ease, and thus the names differ while the meaning remains the same.
The new term is "equanimity" (*upekṣā*), which refers to being free from lethargy and agitation; its meaning is identical to that of the old term.
The new term is "shame" (*hrī*) and "modesty" (*apatrāpya*), whereas the old terms were "tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*) and "mindfulness" (*smṛti*); thus, both the names and their meanings differ.

The new translation refers to the two faculties as non-attachment and non-hatred, while the old translation refers to them as concentration and wisdom; although the names and meanings differ, the underlying principle is largely the same, for it is through these two—concentration and wisdom—that [the state] is accomplished.
Concentration and wisdom also differ in depth; thus, the two faculties are not without their relative superiority and inferiority.
The new translation calls this "non-harming," meaning its nature is the absence of injury or affliction; the old name was "precept" (śīla), so while the names differ, the meaning is the same.
The new term is "diligence" (*vīrya*), while the old term was "progression" (*vīrya*); their meanings are largely the same.

Where the names and meanings differ entirely, this reflects the translator’s distinct intention and need not be harmonized. Here, the emphasis lies in entering contemplation through the name: thus, "skillful kings" and "skillful numbers" together guide various evils to form wondrous goodness. Therefore, the mental factors that assist the king are likewise understood by correlating the numbers with their respective modes of activity (*ākāra*), which should be intelligible accordingly.

If it is so for ten people, then by extending this from ten to all others, even up to an infinite number, they do not go beyond the mental factors (*caitta*). Why then speak only of twelve thousand? Even those who have not yet been converted are entirely subsumed under unwholesome mental factors; why then speak only of the wholesome and the indeterminate?

Regarding the phrase "each of the ten persons is fully prepared" and so forth: this employs the concepts of the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku) to clarify the contemplation of the mind. The fundamental refers to one who has already become a Dharma King; the manifested shows one who has skillfully mastered the realm of the mind. This is done to demonstrate that there are different ways of entering the Path.

Regarding the statement that "within each and every moment of mind there are all the kings," since the two treatises differ, the current claim that they support one another implies simultaneity; it should also be stated that they "arise sequentially."

Not only do they exist simultaneously and at different times, but they also possess various numerical relationships with one another. Because faith possesses all these numerical attributes, it is designated by the name "faith"; the same applies to the other nine.

They receive distinct names based on their predominant quality; thus, the fact that the ten [wholesome mental factors] are universal mental concomitants (*cittasādhāraṇa*) can be understood by this principle.

Therefore, by supporting one another in turn to strike down evil, if one person reforms with a single mind, others will follow; if they support one another, they will all together enter the true realm. Therein, there is nothing that is not the True King—neither king nor non-king, neither number nor non-number. Thus we know that whichever person is particularly strong follows their strength as the object of contemplation, while the weak simply follow along. If one skillfully grasps this meaning, the four modes of conduct and three karmas of cultivation have a basis for practicing contemplation; how much more so when one must discern the similarities and differences between the subject of contemplation and the object?
Regarding the term "jointly attacking," it means that when the mind is generally wholesome, one is immediately able to attack.
Regarding the phrase "does not practice" and so forth, this refers to other unwholesome states; since the capacity to attack belongs to wisdom, it is said that one "practices Prajñā."

Quoting the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*, it states that because both subject and object are exhausted, the mind is without mind and phenomena do not abide in phenomena. To reckon that there is a "capable observer" is called the "self-mind"; because the self-mind exists, subject and object are not extinguished.
If that which belongs to the self (*mama-kāra*) were empty, then sin and merit would have no master.

Regarding the statement, "The mindless and the innumerable are called right contemplation," it is said that "if one does not exhaust [all phenomena], then contemplation is not yet complete"; therefore, it is only upon reaching wondrous enlightenment that it is termed "complete."

That which is called "exhaustion" refers to the exhaustion of the causal mind while the resultant mind is inexhaustible; it is like the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), where the names of cause and effect are identical, yet their essences are eternally distinct.

Citing the intent of various sutras, the phrase "sentient beings are not delivered" and so forth uses a phenomenal event to verify a principle: if the mind that is the object of contemplation does not transform, then the observing sovereign—the mental factors and their primary consciousness—will not cease.

The phrase "and so forth" extensively clarifies the number of kings, the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated, the characteristics of completion and non-completion, and attainment and non-attainment; furthermore, the name "Perfect Enlightenment" (Sambodhi) applies universally to all stages and so on.
Next, regarding the "Enumeration of the Bodhisattva Assembly," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), chapter four, first asks:
What is meant by the term *bodhisattva*?
It answers:
All the dharmas of the Buddhas—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—which are able to benefit all beings, are called *bodhi*;
that mind which is unshakeable, capable of enduring the tasks of attaining the Way, and which neither severs nor destroys, is called a *sattva*.
The text of the response should be explained by way of the three teachings; in contrast to the Small Vehicle, four points are established.
Regarding the passage "Bodhisattvas are those who have left the home life," the *Śāstra* contains two questions. The first question is:
Why is it that in the Śrāvaka sūtras there are the fourfold assembly, yet no Bodhisattvas?
Answer:

There are two kinds of paths, namely those of the śrāvakas and the bodhisattvas. Since the fourfold assembly belongs to the path of the śrāvakas, the śrāvaka sūtras do not contain a bodhisattva assembly.
Next, the question is posed as in the current text, and the answer states:
"While it is thus in a general sense, it is not so in a specific sense; it is as in the current text.
The *Śāstra* asks:
If that is so, why does the Mahāyāna sūtra not list only bodhisattvas?

The intent of this question is as follows: in the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the bodhisattva is not primary; it lists only śrāvakas and the fourfold assembly, with the bodhisattva being included within the fourfold assembly.
In the Mahāyāna, the śrāvaka is not primary; should it not therefore list only bodhisattvas, with the fourfold assembly being subsumed within the category of bodhisattvas?
The *Śāstra* replies:
"This vehicle is so vast that all other vehicles enter it; it is like the Ganges River, which cannot contain the great ocean, whereas the great ocean is able to receive the Ganges."

The intent of the treatise’s response is that it is indeed as you have asked; however, it is merely for the purpose of gathering [practitioners] and gradually leading them toward the Mahāyāna, like entering the ocean step by step. Thus, expedient means are maintained therein. If one relies on the present text to first identify whether the various schools share commonalities or possess distinct differences, only then will one understand the intention behind the assembly of the audience listed in this sutra. It is not the case that the combination or separation of the listed members can distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles, or the Partial and Perfect. For instance, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* lists only those of the Small Vehicle, while the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* lacks both [specific listings of either vehicle]; how could these possibly serve to determine the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles?
Thus we know that one first uses the teaching to establish certainty; when using the teaching to discern individuals, there is not even one error in a hundred cases.
Regarding the phrase "Therefore now," etc., the words are general while the intended meaning is specific.
Regarding the phrase "If it were preserved in full," etc., this first distinguishes between the complete and the abbreviated versions.

Regarding "Bodhi," the following is the formal explanation of its name. First, it is established in relation to the upward-seeking [of enlightenment], and subsequently, it is established in relation to the downward-transforming of others.

*Mahā* (Great) is likewise threefold—great, etc.—compared to what precedes it; it possesses the four teachings, the path, knowledge, and function, and thus is said to be of "many kinds," as detailed in the *Mysterious Meaning* (*Xuanyi*), etc., and within the *Zhi Guan*.

Each of the four great vows is its beginning; each act of benefiting sentient beings is its function; each of the factors of enlightenment is its practice; and each dharma-gate is that which is known.
If the Four Great Vows are distinguished individually, the four [categories] and the three [periods] must necessarily differ;

furthermore, by distinguishing the five flavors, one identifies those who are truly the perfect and subtle Bodhisattvas of this present sutra—just as the *Śāstra* proceeds from the "Exposition" down to the "Ghee," employing the names of the five flavors to differentiate the Bodhisattvas of the four teachings.

The *Treatise* further states: "All that is called 'wholesome dharmas' (kuśala-dharma) is termed *sat*; the essence and characteristics of these wholesome dharmas are termed *tva*. Thus we know that the Bodhisattva’s self-benefit and benefit for others are both wholesome dharmas and the essence and characteristics of wholesomeness; these constitute the fourfold path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is praised by all worthies and sages. This is what is meant by the *sattva* of the fourfold bodhi.
Furthermore, the *Śāstra* states:

"In general discussion, all three types are called *bodhi*, namely the Three Vehicles. Although the persons of the first two vehicles are called *bodhi*, they do not possess the merits of a Buddha; therefore, they are not called *sattva*. Only that which is refined from mixed blood over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and a hundred *kalpas* becomes the pure milk."

Regarding the citation of three passages from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to prove the four flavors: first, the doctrines of the three teachings are used to subsume the four flavors; how much more so now that all five flavors are determined to pertain to Bodhisattvas? Thus, "curd" (*dadhi*) is paired with the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa*), the two types of "ghee" (*ghṛta*) are paired with the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha*), and "clarified butter" (*sarpirmaṇḍa*) is paired with the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).

Because Bodhisattvas pass through these four flavors and enter the indeterminate stage, they correspond in meaning to the Three Contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*): specifically, when a Bodhisattva of the Tripitaka (*piṭaka-traya*) turns toward the Shared Teaching, it corresponds in meaning to the curd stage, as this occurs prior to the Vaipulya period.
When they turn toward the Distinct Teaching, they reside in the [latter] two flavors, because within those two flavors both exist the inconceivable deeds of Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the citation from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*: those who have already entered the reality [of the One Vehicle] perceive the principle of liberation within the two flavors; thus, eight thousand [devas] felt humiliated. To manifest equality with those of dull faculties and the followers of the Two Vehicles, they were rebuked and refined through censure, only then to enter the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) alongside them.

According to the meaning of the text in the *Xuán* (Mysterious) [Commentary], one separates the two flavors to correspond with the general and specific [teachings]; thus, whether advancing or retreating, expanding or contracting, there are two meanings for each.

Therefore, those who enter the reality [of the fruit] all manifest their own bodies like the figures on that throne; the throne is forty-two thousand yojanas high, and the body is likewise of that same measure.
I borrow the intent from the sections on the "Original and Traces" (honji-suijaku) to assist in the provisional teachings (kyōkyō).

Regarding the passage "The doubts of the bodhisattvas are removed," etc., this collectively proves that among the four types of bodhisattvas, those who are provisional must be opened [to the ultimate]. Therefore, it is only in the present sutra that the doubts of the three bodhisattvas are finally removed; only then does one truly practice the Way of a Bodhisattva.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, [the sūtras on] nirvāṇa, etc.," although the two sūtras share the same flavor in that they both cause all aspirations to cease, they are cited together for this reason.
As for the expression "briefly," it refers collectively to both the present and the past.
Regarding "the fundamental and the manifested," there are three parts:

first, clarifying that the fundamental and the manifested are unfathomable; second, from "the reason why" onwards, clarifying the intention behind manifesting the traces; third, from "yet its" onwards, correctly revealing the fundamental to sweep away the traces.

Regarding the phrase "or equal to the Dharma King" in the initial passage: as Manjusri was originally the Buddha Dragon-Species Honored King (Nāga-jāti-agra-rāja), the others may be understood accordingly.

As for "dispersing shadows and manifesting forms," this likewise follows the previous explanation regarding the general clarification of the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku) in relation to the śrāvakas.

Next, regarding the "intention of the traces" (*yìjì*) in the application of the teaching, there are the dharma, the analogy, and the synthesis. Within the analogy, the term "hammer and anvil" is used: the principal teacher of transformation is the hammer, and the assistant is the anvil; even when they act as each other's counterparts, both serve to form a vessel. Originally, the ancient raw material was considered simple and unadorned (*pǔchún*); now, that which has not yet been refined is taken as the simple and unadorned state, so as to cause it to become a vessel—therefore, it is called a "vessel."
Because they are not uniform in their simplicity, they are called "various" (*zhu*).
Within the contemplation (*guan*), what is termed "breaking" (*po*) serves to establish [the realization].

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yunyun*) following the contemplation: one should understand that the five abodes (*wu zhu*) correspond to the three stages (*san ci*) both in sequential and non-sequential order, and the contemplation is likewise to be considered in this way.

Regarding the phrase "conspiring" followed by "and so forth," it should have been illustrated with a metaphor; however, since this opening of the secret treasury does not involve provisional means, those who testify to its faithfulness are not acting on mere impulse, and thus their enumeration in the present text need not be numerous.

Although the assembly is thus arranged, those who attained the Way in the Root Chapter are several times more numerous than in other sutras; specifically, this refers to those who had previously attained the increase of the Path through non-arising. Therefore, one should know that this arrangement is merely according to what is essential.

This clarifies that among those enumerated, they shall already have served as the conditions for this teaching; although it does not explicitly clarify their status in terms of the teachings' provisional or ultimate aspects, since these individuals were privy to the secret deliberations, they must be practitioners of the Perfect Teaching and possess a distant origin.

Regarding the statement "The Eightfold Path is eighty thousand," since it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), there is no member of the path-factors or the Eightfold Path that does not contemplate those ten realms and a thousand suchnesses. Since the ten wholesome actions are the objects of contemplation, the Eightfold Path is the subject of contemplation; as subject and object correspond to one another, each possesses eighty thousand aspects.

Next, in the section clarifying the stages (*bhūmi*), the first part concerns causes and conditions, while the subsequent section beginning with "should [be understood] in four ways" concerns the teaching (*śāsana*).
Regarding the initial passage which states, "within the wondrousness of the object of the unsurpassed path," this refers to the first four of the six objects, namely, the *bodhi*s.
The objects [of cognition] are all that which the wondrous Way tends toward; because the capacity is manifested by means of the object, it is necessary to point to the object.
If one distinguishes the four *siddhāntas*, the three types of non-retrogression constitute the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly);
the merit of entering the stages constitutes the *anuśaṃsa-saṃvṛti* (the production of goodness).
One must certainly cure ignorance, which is the remedial counteraction;
one realizes a portion of the Truth, which is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
The subsequent sections should be understood accordingly; they cannot be recorded in full detail.
Regarding the phrase "one who possesses this name is an avaivartika": *ava* means "non-" or "without," and *vartika* means "retrogression.

Because one attains the three types of non-retrogression prematurely during the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one attains all three meanings simultaneously upon being freed from the five obstacles. This refers to the period spanning the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa up to the hundred kalpas, which encompasses these three forms of non-retrogression.
This is because it is at this point that one is said to have attained "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti).

Next, regarding the six mental states cited for the stage of the Shared Teaching (p’ung-chiao): since there are no distinct stages prior to the grounds (bhūmi) in the Shared Teaching, its positions are established by borrowing the names of the stages from the Distinct Teaching (pieh-chiao). This refers specifically to entering the Stage of Dry Wisdom (kan-hui-wei) from the seventh level of faith (shin) and above in the Distinct Teaching; therefore, it is said that from the first ground up to the sixth ground, one is designated as having "non-retrogression of position" (wei-pu-tui).

Alternatively, some refer to the seven sages conventionally established prior to the stages [of the path of seeing], taking the stage of *kṣānti* (patience) as the sixth mind; although this is called the "stage of non-retrogression" according to the Śrāvaka vehicle, when compared to the Bodhisattva vehicle, it is still termed "retrogression."
Next, regarding the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it is not refuted here because it accords with the masters of the *Dilun* school.

As for the Perfect Stage (*yuanwei*), no teaching’s presentation of the perfect stages surpasses that of the *Avataṃsaka*. Although other texts contain references to such stages, their meaning is not fully revealed; they may briefly mention only the first stage (*chuzhu*) while omitting the subsequent stages. If this is the case for the first stage, how could the practices of the stages of progression (*xingxiang*) be any different?
How could it be the same as the delusions previously suppressed prior to the stages?

Furthermore, regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, the stages following [the first] include both the distinct (vyatibhinna) and the universal; yet some interpret this solely according to the sequential (krama), while others interpret it solely according to the perfect and sudden (yugapad). How mistaken this is!

Regarding "possessing the three non-regressions": if one were to explain them by assigning them sequentially to the stages prior to this, then the seventh stage of faith would be called "non-regression in position," from the eighth stage of faith onward it would be called "non-regression in practice," and from the first dwelling (bhūmi) onward it would be called "non-regression in mindfulness. Now, since one possesses these three virtues starting from the first dwelling, they are termed the "three non-regressions"; thus, it is said that one "possesses" them.
Prajñā is the state, for it is free from the two types of death;
liberation is the practice, for it is endowed with all conditioned activities;
the Dharma-body is called mindfulness, for it realizes the realm of ultimate reality.

The characteristics of this are explained in detail within the seventh chapter, "The Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*), of that sutra. At the beginning of the scroll, Śakra asks Dharmamati:
"How many dharmas and how many treasuries of merit does one accomplish upon entering the first stage?"
Dharmamati replied:
"This matter is profoundly deep; it is difficult to believe and difficult to know, difficult to explain and difficult to understand, difficult to penetrate and difficult to discern.
Nevertheless, relying upon the Buddha's power, I shall expound it in full; yet first, let us make a comparison:"

If one were to provide all the requisites for happiness to incalculable sentient beings throughout the ten directions for a thousand kalpas and further cause them to realize the state of a Pratyekabuddha, this would not equal even a hundred-thousand-billionth part of [the merit of] the former.
Furthermore, it is said:

"If one wishes to know that the worlds of the ten directions are one yet many, and many yet one, and that a single thought-moment is equal to immeasurable thought-moments, [the merit of] bestowing [the Dharma] upon beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth across four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—as described in the *Lotus Sūtra*, even to the point of enabling them to attain the stage of no-more-learning—is not equal to that of the person who first rejoiced [in the teaching]. That sūtra still regards such [attainment] as being within the ranks of the holy ones; therefore, it speaks of 'the ten directions' and so forth."

If one contemplates the merit of a single thought-moment of this fiftieth person, only then is revealed the inconceivability of the perfect stage (*yuanwei*); this scripture is difficult to fathom. Since both are the Perfect Teaching where beginning and end are non-dual, how can there be "this" or "that"?

Regarding the phrase "not even the first abode," these bodhisattvas are all those in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha); they are already ancient Buddhas, let alone being at the first abode.

Since the time of the new translations, the positions of Yogācāra-Vijñaptimātra have merely obscured the teachings of the perfect and eternal *Avataṃsaka*; who would have known that the texts on Vijñaptimātra and the like only clarify distinct stages?
Who among future generations would be willing to discern these similarities and differences?
Furthermore, there are those who utterly destroy the provisional school of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; such individuals are completely deluded regarding the path of skillful means.

Regarding "not recognizing the traces": since these traces occupy the forefront of all sutras and extend to the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, can one not verify from this that they belong to those at a shallow stage?
Having already lost its fundamental basis and being confused regarding its manifestations, how much more so when judging according to the various schools?

Since the schools are subtle and the person [the Buddha] is honored, and the various masters do not understand the five periods, how can they know the fundamental and manifested aspects of the Bodhisattva?
Therefore, it is said: "That which is praised is already erroneous," and so forth.

Since praising the Universal (the *samdhā-bhāṣita*) by means of the Treasuries (*pitaka*) has already constituted a fault, the error of praising the Partial (the *neyārtha*) by means of the Perfect (the *nītārtha*) is even greater.

Regarding the phrase "it results in the two slanders of increase and decrease": this single instance of error incurs two faults; for while the Sūtra contains no threefold teaching [to be added], one would increase it through a forced desire, and by suppressing the Perfect to establish the Partial, how could the error exceed this?

Regarding "the three contemplations are the three non-regressions": the one mind of emptiness, provisional practice, and the middle [truth] is still based upon the wondrous threefold contemplation being fully present in each.

The phrase "and so forth" refers to a detailed explanation of the characteristics of sequential and non-sequential [realization], as well as how a single thought-moment must be understood in terms of the six stages of realization.

Regarding the phrase "extremely possessing eyebrows and eyes," although it appears to grant [the existence of] eyebrows and eyes, it actually takes them away; despite the presence of eyebrows and eyes, the fundamental substance is entirely absent.
From the section beginning with "examining and discussing" (*he lun*) onwards, it is a negation.

Regarding "no progression": in what teachings are these manifested virtues and so forth absent? Although it is said that the Dharma-body and Reward-body do not distinguish between the Perfect and Distinct [Teachings], if one were to differentiate between the Perfect and Distinct as earlier or later, or even whether the various phrases are horizontal or vertical?
Therefore, it is refuted in general by stating that there is no essential substance (*svabhāva*) to the thesis (*pakṣa*).

If there were such an essential substance to the thesis, then those who have realized the stages (*bhūmi*) would establish their positions based on the sūtras; the basis upon which these positions rest is called the "root of the position" (*bhūmi-mūla*), and this root is the essence (*svabhāva*), while the position itself is the thesis. Moreover, since this present sūtra specifically transcends all other teachings and all other stages, the meaning of its praise of virtues according to the teaching can be understood accordingly.
Therefore, beginning with non-retrogression and culminating in the salvation of sentient beings, one must first establish the essence and the doctrine before praising its virtues.
Question:
Why does this sutra vertically praise the stages of the separate teaching’s ten bhūmis?
Answer:
First, the reliance on the source; second, the verification of identity; third, the conformity with the treatise.
Regarding the question, "What is the seventh stage? and so forth:

The ancient masters’ judgment that the seventh stage might give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles seems to refer to the common (pervasive) stages; therefore, it is difficult to establish the distinct meaning [of the separate teaching], and the same applies to the difficulty of establishing the perfect [teaching].

If it is said that one first enters the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) at the seventh stage, this is the explicit meaning of the *vyavasthita-śāsana* (distinctive teaching); therefore, it does not constitute the Perfect [Teaching].

Regarding the phrase "advancing and retreating" and so forth, "advancing" is rejected because it does not achieve the Perfect, and "retreating" refers to what is neither the Common nor the Distinct [teachings].

Regarding the "horizontal and vertical" (heng-shu) structure of the current text: the vertical section praises the fundamental intent of the text, which lies in its perfection (yuan). First, there is the direct explanation; second, the analytical examination.

Within the initial vertical section, although the first passage borrows the terminology of "leaving behind the two," it must differ from the *Yingluo Jing*, where the two are treated as expedient means (*upāya*). Here, one still relies on the single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) possessing the three non-regressions as the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). It is the perfect departure from the three defilements, the perfect arousal of the three wisdoms, the perfect clarity and perfect turning. To perfectly plant the roots of virtue through a single thought-moment of offering is the perfect praise of the Buddha; that he possesses the three perfect compassions and the non-dual Buddha-wisdom is to be understood accordingly in what follows.

If one does not distinguish the state of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), then all four lines would equally praise the ten stages (daśabhūmi); however, since the explanation here follows the method of distinguishing them, the latter three lines praise Equal Enlightenment.
As for the mention of "two lines" in the text, this refers to the eleventh and twelfth lines, which describe the internal and external virtues of the ten stages.
However, because they are not complete from the very beginning, they appear to be distinct.

Furthermore, regarding the first phrase in the subsequent horizontal praise, which also says "transcending the two extremes": if even in the vertical sense they are both perfectly complete, how much more so in this horizontal praise that transcends the two extremes?
It is merely established as "vertical" based on what is not vertical, as previously explained.

Regarding the phrase "transcending the two extremes": coarse afflictions have already been eliminated; furthermore, the name is established from the standpoint of the superior [stage]. All subsequent phrases should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the term "A-ji" (the letter A), its current lineage-based application is fully detailed in the fifth commentary of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

As for the question and answer: in the initial question, the first phrase establishes the thesis; the section beginning with "the Three Baskets" provisionally grants the premise; the section beginning with "śrāvakas" establishes an analogy; and the section beginning with "traces as... sets forth the objection.
The intent of establishing this thesis is to demonstrate the severance of delusions.

From the stages of "dwelling" (bhūmi) upward, these praises of virtue are all made in reference to the stages of severance according to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). Since the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka (sanzang) do not sever [delusions] from beginning to end, they would not be praised in that manner.

If one already praises the Two Vehicles even within the context of severing delusions, how could one not praise those Bodhisattvas who, through their provisional and distinct tracks, sever delusions? Yet, both the horizontal and vertical praises are exclusively praises of the Perfect [Teaching].

The meaning of the reply is that while the principle (*artha*) applies to both the original and the trace, the intent (*abhiprāya*) lies solely in the Perfect [Teaching]. Although the vertical text seems to praise the Distinct [Teaching], according to the specific scripture (*piṭaka*), it praises only the Perfect; thus, one borrows the trace to explain the text while the scriptural intent follows the original. Therefore, following the praise of the śrāvakas from the perspective of the trace, one should likewise praise the Bodhisattvas across all four teachings; however, because one wishes to know the essential purport of the Perfect, one discards the trace to preserve the original, and sets aside the beginning to take up the end.
Next is the question regarding what is visible.
The response consists of three parts:
first, the direct answer.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "The old [translation] says," it cites the distinct stages as examples; since the eight stages have not yet reached the ultimate, there is no doubt that the old interpretation still possesses these virtues. Why, then, should it hinder us from maintaining that for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), every single stage is fully endowed with all virtues?
Third, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fahua lun) provides the scriptural citations.
The *Śāstra* states:

"The virtues of that bodhisattva are subsumed within thirteen phrases and two textual sections; one should know that these consist of: first, the gate of the upper and lower branches, and second, the gate of the subsumption of matters."

The "upper and lower branches" at the beginning refer to the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). One should know that from the beginning up to "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*) constitutes the general [category], while the remainder are the specific ones.

That *Śāstra* states: "There are ten kinds of manifestations of non-retrogression," as cited in full above; however, with the exception of the initial general phrase, there are twelve phrases. These are reduced to ten manifestations by combining the two phrases on "making offerings" and "planting merit" into the fourth manifestation, and combining the two phrases on "renown" and "delivering sentient beings" into the tenth manifestation. Thus, they constitute exactly ten manifestations, all of which are named after non-retrogression.

Therefore, one should know that in this perfect exposition, each phrase interpenetrates the others; every single manifestation fully possesses the ten manifestations and all the phrases. How could it be otherwise than for the ten manifestations to comprise twelve phrases?
This is identical in intent to the "Forty-two Letter Gate" (dvācatvāriṃśadakṣaramukha).

Furthermore, regarding the scriptural passage on "cultivating the body through loving-kindness" (*maitrī*), the treatise explains that both physical and mental actions are fully cultivated therein. The reason the scripture briefly mentions only the cultivation of the mind is that loving-kindness is itself the mind; since the mind perfumes the body, they are not mentioned separately.

Moreover, because one does not regress by relying on the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), we know that both the stages (*bhūmi*) and the dwellings (*vihāra*) realize both forms of emptiness.

Regarding why the vertical explanation of the text, though distinct in its phrasing, is not distinct in its underlying intent: first, because there is subsequent text that explains horizontally, this horizontal explanation is based on the vertical structure; second, it relies on the meaning of each sentence in the *Śāstra* to correspond to the various stages (*bhūmi*), as in the case of the First Stage, which states that one does not fall into the two extremes and is fully endowed with the three contemplations, simultaneously illuminating both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as existence and non-existence.
Whether it be merit or wisdom, neither is separate from the single mind; how could the internal causes and external conditions ever fail to be complete?

Since this is so for the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is likewise for all subsequent stages. Within this very stage, they are fully present both horizontally and vertically; yet, provisional stage-names are borrowed to correspond to a sequential progression. To reveal that [the reality] is exclusively perfect (*yuan*), one must provide a horizontal interpretation.

Therefore, the "Gate of Encompassing Phenomena" (*vastu-mukha*) within the *Śāstra* should be explained through vertical exposition; for this reason, the present text employs both gates from the *Śāstra* for its explanation. However, following the *Śāstra*, the two characters "what kind of" (*he deng*) have been omitted from the phrase "in what kind of object" (*he deng jing jie*) in the current text.
The *Śāstra* merely states:
"Because one should perform what is to be done within a certain sphere of objects.
The *Śāstra* itself explains this as follows:

Regarding the phrase "the purity of the stages," it refers to the tranquility and purity of the signless practice (*animitta-caryā*) across the three stages from the eighth stage upward. The meaning of the present text follows the statement in that *Śāstra* regarding what the "three things" are, assigning each one to the various stages: "purity" refers to the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*) in the various stages; "expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to the progressive advancement through the various stages; "objective sphere" (*viṣaya*) refers to the basis upon which the various stages rely; and "that which should be accomplished" (*sādhyam*) refers to the functional efficacy (*kāritra*) of the various stages.
The *Śāstra* states:
"Regarding skillful means (*upāya*), there are four kinds:

first, the skillful means of grasping the sublime Dharma, which consists of upholding the sublime Dharma and expounding it for others through the power of eloquence. This corresponds to the first four lines; reflect upon them according to their meaning.

"Second is the skillful means of embracing virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), because one should perform what ought to be done by relying upon virtuous friends. This refers to the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth lines; reflect upon them according to each line.
"Third is the skillful means of gathering sentient beings, because one does not abandon them"—this refers to the ninth phrase.
"Fourth is the skillful means of gathering wisdom, because one teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they may enter that wisdom"—this refers to the final four phrases.
Since each phrase already corresponds [to its respective stage], what further does "what kind" (ji-deng) mean?
"What kind" is a term used for differentiation.
Here, they are also mutually interpenetrating; each skillful means universally encompasses the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), in accordance with various sūtras and śāstras.

Furthermore, in the *Ālokālaṃkāra* (Yíngluò), it is stated that from the first bhūmi upward, one enters the "flow of the Dharma" (*dharmasrotas*) and, because one advances moment by moment, enters the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyāmārga*).

The *Śāstra* also contains matters concerning the "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) and the manifestation of various stages and grounds; however, as these are not essential to the sūtra, they will not be further discussed here.

Regarding the mention of the "Eight Stages" (aṣṭabhūmi), although it does not appear in the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra*, it is not absent from other sūtras; furthermore, as it represents a distinct doctrinal interpretation within the intermediate teaching, one may either adopt or reject it as one sees fit. For now, we shall follow the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra*, as this does not significantly contradict the *Śāstra* and is thus adopted according to the tradition of our own school.

Regarding the phrase "what kind of realm," this refers to the sphere where one benefits sentient beings. Next, concerning the contemplation of the mind: here, the preceding text describes the ancient tradition and refutes the old interpretation as being based on causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);

the current text provides two interpretations of the meaning as pertaining to the teaching and contemplation (*shikyo*). Although the "original" and "traced" aspects (*honjaku*) are omitted, since virtue follows the person, they are not explained again. The three contemplations (*sankan*) are without distinction, though their names differ according to the specific matter. If this is so, these various phrases are also mutually inclusive of one another: because one attains the non-retrogressive single-mind three-contemplations (*ichinen sankan*), one then attains the single-mind three-contemplations for saving sentient beings; and because one attains the single-mind three-contemplations for saving sentient beings, one then attains the non-retrogressive single-mind three-contemplations. The intermediate phrases may be understood accordingly.

One should know that these one hundred phrases are in fact but a single phrase; therefore, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, the positions are perfectly interfused. Since the individual phrases share the same meaning, there is no need for convoluted interpretation.

Within the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), when the Buddha opened up the beginning of this single phrase’s meaning for Śāriputra, Śāriputra himself declared it to be inexhaustible; how much more so, then, can the virtues of this Perfect Bodhisattva be divided and fixed as distinct categories?
Moreover, since the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) is itself its very virtue, how could one doubt that the fusion of contemplation and virtue is sublime?
Therefore, it should be explained by way of the mastery of the various phrases.
Someone asks:
Why is Mañjuśrī placed at the head in this text?
Answer:

Since he was able to resolve Maitreya’s doubts within the introduction, he serves as the primary initiator of this entire sutra; moreover, as he raised these doubts before twenty thousand Buddhas for the sake of the assembly, he is therefore listed at the head of the eighty thousand [bodhisattvas].
Regarding the phrase "Dharma-gates" (*dharmaparyāya*) and so forth, based on the principles of these names and meanings, there should be four types of exegesis;

however, that fewer are presented here is because one can infer them by analogy. Furthermore, the deeds of Bodhisattvas may be hidden or manifest, real or conventional, primary or auxiliary, unlike the deeds of Śrāvakas which are prominent. Although not prominent, they necessarily encompass all teachings, yet the meaning revealed here must reside in the Perfect [Teaching] (*pariniṣpanna*). Moreover, as previously explained through the general and specific expositions concerning the Śrāvakas, one has already come to know the fundamental and manifested aspects (*honjaku*) of the Bodhisattvas. Since this is the case for their fundamental and manifested aspects, the causal conditions, teachings, and contemplations can be understood by analogy; therefore, I shall not describe the general and specific aspects of the Bodhisattvas in detail.
