Now, regarding the first section on Mañjuśrī, five passages are cited: the first three distinguish his names; the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* (or *Siddhārthasūtra*) cites his explanations to clarify his practice; and the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* discusses his vows to benefit sentient beings.

Regarding the first term, "Mahā-sūtra" (The Great Sutra): its name is established based on virtue; specifically, the name "Wonderful Virtue" (Sudhana) is established because he has realized his nature. This follows the text of the vow made by King Ajātaśatru after his repentance in the seventeenth chapter.
The following two sūtras merely cite differences in the Sanskrit pronunciation.

The *Samparigraha-sūtra* clarifies that one should contemplate according to what is taught; "contemplation" (guan) refers to not giving rise to notions of "dharmas" or "non-dharmas. Contemplation is itself practice; thus, when words and actions accord with one another, one attains a sublime reputation.

In the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, because he took up a wondrous land and extensively benefited sentient beings, the scope of his transformation was vast and the rank of those transformed was high; since his lofty and expansive vows and practices were all sublime, he was named "Sublime Virtue" (Miaode).
By what cause are the traces of the Bodhisattva’s benefiting of sentient beings determined? Within this text, one may also establish an interpretation through the four *siddhāntas*.

That is to say, whether in name or substance, nothing regarding Wondrous Virtue (*Mañjuśrī*) is other than the four *siddhāntas*: taking up the land is the world-view; preaching the Dharma is for humans; establishing practice is the remedial view; and the Buddha’s prediction and so forth are the ultimate truth. This concerns the person of the Perfect Teaching; furthermore, it should be analyzed according to the teachings, from "the northern direction" onwards, which refers to the fundamental and the manifested.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Dragon-Seed Supreme Honored King; he was also Mañjuśrī."

Regarding the four *siddhāntas* within the context of Avalokiteśvara: "name" refers to the world (*loka*), "benefiting others" refers to the person (*pudgala*), "invoking the name" refers to remediation (*pratipakṣa*), and the departure of the "Buddha Ratnagarbha" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃcodana-sūtra* (Siyi jing) states that attaining bodhi is also the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The phrase "the following text" refers to the "Universal Gateway Chapter" (*Pumen pin*).

Regarding the note "and so forth," it is also missing an explanation in terms of the teaching (*jiao*) and its fundamental and manifest aspects (*benji*); as for the teaching, this refers to those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), whose original nature is that of ancient Buddhas.

In the commentary on the first two characters of "contemplating the mind" (*guan xin*), there is no difference from what follows; however, the third character differs slightly from below. Below, the explanation is based on phenomena (*dharma*), taking that which is addressed as "sound" (*yin*); here, it is based on the contemplating subject, taking that which is proclaimed as "sound. Since the establishment of the teaching arises from contemplation, it is said: "Contemplation is the root of speech."

Next, regarding Mahāsthāmaprāpta: the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* explains him in terms of practice, while the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* explains him in terms of vows. The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* explains "power" (*sthāma*) by means of majestic power (*vega*), which precisely accords with the literal meaning of the character.

Regarding "taking up the great trichiliocosm," this refers to the power of his worldly influence; he takes hold of the world through his power without contradicting his resolve. Because his resolve is so vast, the Buddha bestowed this prediction upon him.
Because its aspiration takes worldly matters as its object, it is also called "worldly aspiration.

If one establishes the four *siddhāntas*, this corresponds to the world-enriching (*lokasaṃdarśana*) and the person-enriching (*pudgalaviniścaya*) for the purpose of remediation; the "Buddha Ratnagarbha" represents the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It also lacks the provisional teaching (*kyōjō*).
The relationship between the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*) can be understood by applying the preceding pattern to what follows;
however, the text is missing. Regarding "constant diligence," as stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*:

"This bodhisattva follows after a single sentient being for immeasurable eons without abandoning them; even if that being does not accept transformation, the bodhisattva does not relinquish them for even a single thought-moment, because they advance with both body and mind."
The meaning [of this] applies to all four *siddhāntas*; the traces of the teaching and the contemplation of the mind may be understood by analogy.
As for "unresting" (*aniśrita*), its general intent is roughly the same as that of "constant diligence" (*nityavīrya*).

To distinguish between them: entering [the path] without interruption is called "diligence," while being without cessation over a long duration is called "unresting. Therefore, the contemplative understanding is termed "non-abiding"; thus, the explanation of "unresting" also pertains to the long duration, differing only in that it concerns receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) versus benefiting sentient beings.
The traces of the teaching may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the explanation of "Precious Hand" (*ratnapāṇi*), first the hand is explained, and then from "causes it to be explained" onwards, the preciousness is explained.

"Hand" refers to a part of the body; since his body parts have been made firm by donning the aforementioned armor, he uses that firm hand to produce the unsurpassed supramundane jewel even from a portion of the *dharmakāya*, let alone a worldly jewel.

Therefore, these two treasures must both possess the four *siddhāntas*. Within this context, the phrase "not aspiring to the Two Vehicles" serves to distinguish the Dharma-treasure from its potential confusion with other categories.
As for "the mind of penetrating wisdom," it arises from reality as penetration; since penetration is the very nature of wisdom, it is called "penetrating wisdom."
Regarding the various discussions on the provisional and definitive teachings, as well as the primary and secondary aspects (*honjaku*), within the commentary on the "Medicine King" chapter:

the three conditions follow the meaning of the "King of Physicians," which corresponds to medicine. Although the first two are distinct, they both establish practice to generate goodness during the Buddha’s lifetime and after his parinirvāṇa.

Regarding "Purification by Fire" (*aggiparicariyā*): this name is established based on the practice of burning the body; in the text, it is used as a worldly metaphor to represent supramundane purification, and so forth.
As for the "seven missing bodhisattvas," I have not yet been able to verify them in the sūtras.
Within the name Bhadrapāla, the first phrase refers to the world (*loka*), while from "Sikṣāsamuccaya" (*Siddhārthamati*) downward, it refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This Bodhisattva is also named Bhadrapāla in the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*; "Bhadra" means "virtuous," and "pāla" signifies skillfully protecting [the practitioner] so that they do not regress.

In the *Maitreya-sūtra*, the first phrase refers to the world (*loka*); in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samantabhadrotsāhana-parivarta*, it refers to the benefit of persons (*pudgala-artha*); in the *Bhadra-śrī-sūtra*, it is the remedy (*pratipakṣa*); and in the *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, it is said that "departure" (*niḥsaraṇa*) should properly be included within the category of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Wise and the Foolish," it is the ninth chapter of that sutra. While the Buddha was at Kalandaka, Ānanda suddenly reflected:
"How did the World-Honored One Maitreya, in the past, give rise to this heart of compassion and attain such wondrous benefit?"
Rising from meditative concentration, he addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"In the distant past, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Mahāpuruṣa who ruled over five hundred small kingdoms. While out hunting with his ministers, the king’s elephant became overcome by a fierce lustful desire. Seeing a mahout training an elephant, the king immediately conceived a resolve, vowing that he would now become one who occupies the place of succession."

Furthermore, there is also a sūtra passage concerning the story of the lame rabbit that was not yet saved, which establishes the designation of "compassion" (maitrī); through the permeation of the power of his original vow, he gives rise to compassion upon seeing suffering.

In the previous *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the bestowing of happiness was explained by means of the extraction of suffering; therefore, it is said that perfect extraction and bestowal are non-distinct in essence.
The phrase "and so forth" refers to the teachings concerning the origin and trace, the contemplation of the mind, and even the mobilization of the assembly in the Trace Gate.

Regarding the explanation of "Guide," the text employs the four *siddhāntas*. The Guide was a native of Śrāvastī and was a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*); "causing others to enter the right path" explains the character for "guide" (*nāyaka*), while "not seeking gratitude or recompense" explains the virtue of a "teacher" (*śāstṛ*). It is precisely because he has abandoned all worldly attachment that he is worthy of the rank of a teacher.

Regarding those cases where only numbers are listed instead of specific names, the underlying principles—such as the contemplation of causes and conditions—are identical to those previously explained; however, because the names are too numerous to be fully enumerated, only the major figures are indicated.
In short, those among the people who previously possessed extensive knowledge are listed first; it is easier to verify their credentials.

Regarding the great bodhisattvas within the teachings of this dispensation who obtained predictions based on their past affinities, these are mostly found in the second fascicle of the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The Sūtra says:
"There was a bodhisattva named Śāntamati who addressed the Buddha, saying:
'All Buddhas possess pure lands; for what reason has the Tathāgata taken this defiled land?'"
The Buddha said:
"It was taken by virtue of my original vow.

In the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in an aeon called 'Good' (Bhadra) and in a world named 'Sāṃdṛṣṭika,' there was a wheel-turning monarch named 'Araṇemin. He ruled over the four continents and had a thousand sons."

There was a great minister named the Brahmacārin Ratnasāgara, who had an only son endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence. Constantly attended by various devas who came to make offerings, the kingdom gave him the name Ratnagarbha. Upon leaving the household life and attaining the Way, he was also called Ratnagarbha; he preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings in numbers beyond measure.

The king’s thousand sons each made offerings for three months; when the three months had passed, he wished to bestow upon them their predictions of enlightenment. First, he entered samādhi and manifested the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, gathering all the bodhisattvas there, and first bestowed the prediction upon Ratnasāgara.
As for those who have taught the ocean-like assembly of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they shall all attain Buddhahood simultaneously.

Next, he conferred upon him the position of a Universal Monarch with a thousand sons. To the eldest son, he said: "Observe the six realms of existence and give rise to great compassion; sever all afflictions and cause them to abide in peace and happiness. From now on, I shall name you Avalokiteśvara. After Amitābha Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpas, at the end of the first watch of the night when the True Dharma is extinguished, and at the beginning of the last watch of the night, this land will change its name to the Supreme Realm of Peace and Happiness Adorned with All Manner of Precious Jewels. In a single thought-moment, you shall attain perfect enlightenment, and your title shall be King of the Mountain of All Merits. Your lifespan shall be ninety-six billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas."

The second prince was named Mahāsthāmaprāpta, as recorded in the commentary; the third was named Mañjuśrī, as recorded in the commentary; the fourth was named Samantabhadra, who resided in worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten *gaṅgā*-sands of worlds in the eastern direction, in a world named Animiṣa; continuing in this sequence up to the ninth, named Akṣobhya, he thus conferred [the position] upon a thousand princes.
Among them, there was one who made a vow to attain Buddhahood in the five turbidities; because of his great compassion, his land is named Sahā. Why is this?
Because the sentient beings therein endure the three poisons and all afflictions; since they can endure such evils, it is called the Land of Endurance (Kṣānti).
"Among these thousand people, with the exception of only one, all the others shall attain Buddhahood within the Bhadrakalpa.
— *Fahua Wenju*, Fascicle 2.
